title: Chunking, Indexing, and Retrieval Strategies
monthTitle: Building RAG Applications with Vector Databases
summary: Learn how to split documents into effective chunks, index them in a vector database, and tune retrieval so your RAG app returns the most relevant context for each query. Covers chunking strategies, embeddings, indexing parameters, and retrieval techniques like top-k, hybrid search, metadata filtering, and re-ranking.
objectives: Choose an appropriate chunking strategy (size, overlap, structure-aware) for a given document type
Explain how embeddings and vector indexes (HNSW, IVF) affect retrieval quality and speed
Configure retrieval parameters such as top-k, similarity metric, and metadata filters
Apply hybrid search and re-ranking to improve relevance over pure vector similarity
Diagnose and fix common retrieval failures using evaluation metrics

options: To reduce the total number of vectors stored
To preserve context that would otherwise be cut at chunk boundaries
To make embeddings faster to compute
To force the LLM to read more text
quiz.why: Overlap repeats some tokens from the previous chunk so meaning spanning a boundary isn't lost, improving retrieval of split-up context.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of hybrid search over pure vector search?
options: It removes the need for an embedding model
It catches exact terms, names, and codes that embeddings often miss
It eliminates the need for chunking
quiz.why: Hybrid search combines dense vector similarity with sparse keyword/BM25 matching, so exact tokens like product codes or acronyms are reliably retrieved.

quiz.q: Which is a correct way to use a re-ranker in retrieval?
options: Retrieve top-1 then re-rank that single result
Retrieve a large candidate set (e.g., 20-50), re-rank, keep the best few
Skip vector search entirely and only re-rank
quiz.why: Re-ranking works by pulling a broad candidate set with fast ANN search, then scoring query-passage pairs with a cross-encoder to keep the most relevant few.

quiz.q: You change your chunk size from 800 to 400 tokens. What else must you do?
quiz.why: New chunk boundaries produce different text, so all chunks must be re-embedded and the index rebuilt to reflect the new chunks.

quiz.q: Name one retrieval metric you would track to evaluate whether the correct passage is being retrieved.
quiz.why: Recall@k (or hit rate) measures whether the expected source chunk appears in the top k retrieved results, directly evaluating retrieval correctness.

quiz.q: Why must you use the same embedding model for both documents and queries?
quiz.answer: So query and document vectors live in the same vector space and are comparable
quiz.why: Different models produce incompatible vector spaces; similarity scores between them are meaningless, breaking retrieval.

body_markdown:
## Why Chunking and Retrieval Matter

A Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) app is only as good as the context it feeds the LLM. If retrieval returns irrelevant or fragmented passages, the model hallucinates or answers vaguely. Two levers control retrieval quality: **how you split documents (chunking)** and **how you search the index (retrieval strategy)**.

The pipeline is: `documents -> chunks -> embeddings -> vector index -> query -> retrieve -> (re-rank) -> context -> LLM`.

## Chunking Strategies

Chunking splits long documents into passages small enough to embed and fit in the prompt, but large enough to carry meaning.

- **Fixed-size chunking**: split by a token/character count (e.g., 512 tokens). Simple and fast, but can cut sentences mid-thought.
- **Overlap**: include the last N tokens of the previous chunk (e.g., 10-20% overlap) so context isn't lost at boundaries.
- **Recursive/structure-aware chunking**: split on natural separators in order — paragraphs, then sentences, then words. Keeps semantic units intact.
- **Document-structure chunking**: respect Markdown headings, HTML tags, code blocks, or PDF sections so each chunk maps to a logical unit.
- **Semantic chunking**: group sentences by embedding similarity, breaking when topic shifts.

### Rules of thumb

- Start with **~300-800 tokens** per chunk and **10-15% overlap**.
- Smaller chunks = more precise retrieval but more fragments and higher index cost.
- Larger chunks = more context per hit but more noise and risk of diluting the embedding.
- Attach **metadata** (source, title, section, page, date) to every chunk for filtering and citations.

## Embeddings and Indexing

Each chunk is converted to a vector by an embedding model (e.g., `text-embedding-3-small`). Choose an embedding model that matches your domain and language, and **use the same model for queries and documents**.

Vector databases store these vectors in an **Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN)** index for fast search:

- **HNSW** (graph-based): great recall/latency balance; tune `M` (connections) and `ef_search` (search breadth).
- **IVF** (cluster-based): partitions vectors into lists; tune `nprobe` (lists searched).
- **Flat / brute force**: exact but slow; fine for small datasets.

Similarity is measured with **cosine**, **dot product**, or **Euclidean** distance — pick what your embedding model was trained for (usually cosine).

## Retrieval Strategies

- **Top-k retrieval**: return the k most similar chunks. Typical k = 3-8. Too low misses context; too high adds noise and cost.
- **Metadata filtering**: restrict search by source, date, or user permissions before/while searching.
- **Hybrid search**: combine dense (vector) and sparse (keyword/BM25) retrieval to catch exact terms, names, and acronyms that embeddings miss.
- **Re-ranking**: retrieve a larger candidate set (e.g., 20-50), then use a cross-encoder re-ranker to score query-passage pairs and keep the best few.
- **Query transformations**: rewrite, expand, or split the user query (multi-query, HyDE) to improve recall.
- **MMR (Maximal Marginal Relevance)**: balances relevance with diversity to avoid near-duplicate chunks.

## Putting It Together (Example)

```python
from langchain_text_splitters import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter

splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=600, chunk_overlap=80,
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " "]
)
chunks = splitter.split_documents(docs)

# index chunks with metadata, then retrieve
results = vector_store.similarity_search(
    query, k=20, filter={"source": "handbook"}
)
top = reranker.rerank(query, results)[:5]
```

## Evaluating and Tuning

Don't guess — measure. Build a small set of question/expected-source pairs and track:

- **Recall@k / Hit rate**: did the right chunk appear in the top k?
- **Context precision**: how much retrieved text is actually relevant?
- **Faithfulness/answer quality**: does the final answer rely on retrieved context?

Tune one variable at a time: chunk size, overlap, k, hybrid weighting, re-ranking. Re-embed when you change chunking or the embedding model.

## Common Pitfalls

- Mismatched query/document embedding models.
- Chunks too large (noisy embeddings) or too small (lost context).
- No metadata, so no filtering or citations.
- Relying on pure vector search for exact-match queries (IDs, codes) — add keyword/hybrid.
- Forgetting to re-index after changing chunking parameters.

slides.narration: Welcome. In this lesson we'll learn how to make a RAG application return the most relevant context for any query. Retrieval quality depends on two things you control: how you split your documents into chunks, and how you search the index. We'll cover both, plus how to measure and tune them.

slides.title: The RAG Retrieval Pipeline
bullets: Documents → chunks → embeddings → vector index
Query → search → retrieve → optional re-rank → context → LLM
Bad retrieval = hallucinations and vague answers
Chunking and retrieval are the two biggest quality levers
slides.narration: A RAG app is only as good as the context it feeds the model. The pipeline starts by splitting documents into chunks, embedding them, and storing them in a vector index. At query time we embed the question, search the index, optionally re-rank, and pass the best passages to the LLM. If retrieval returns junk, the model hallucinates. So chunking and retrieval are where we focus our tuning effort.

slides.title: Chunking Strategies
bullets: Fixed-size: simple but cuts sentences mid-thought
Overlap: carry 10-15% of previous chunk to keep context
Recursive/structure-aware: split on paragraphs then sentences
Semantic: break when topic shifts
Always attach metadata (source, section, page, date)
slides.narration: Chunking splits long documents into passages. The simplest approach is fixed-size by token count, but it can cut sentences in half. Adding overlap preserves context across boundaries. Recursive splitting respects natural separators like paragraphs and sentences, keeping meaning intact. Semantic chunking breaks where the topic changes. Whatever you choose, attach metadata to every chunk so you can filter and cite later.

slides.title: Chunk Size: Rules of Thumb
bullets: Start with ~300-800 tokens, 10-15% overlap
Smaller = precise retrieval, more fragments, higher cost
Larger = more context per hit, but more noise
Tune empirically per document type
slides.narration: For sizing, start around 300 to 800 tokens with 10 to 15 percent overlap. Smaller chunks give precise retrieval but create many fragments and higher indexing cost. Larger chunks pack more context into each hit but dilute the embedding with noise. There's no universal answer — tune it for your document type and measure the impact.

slides.title: Embeddings and Indexing
bullets: Use the SAME embedding model for queries and documents
ANN indexes: HNSW (graph) and IVF (clusters)
Tune HNSW ef_search / M; IVF nprobe for recall vs speed
Pick the right similarity: cosine, dot, or Euclidean
slides.narration: Each chunk becomes a vector via an embedding model — and you must use the same model for both documents and queries. Vector databases store these in approximate-nearest-neighbor indexes. HNSW is graph-based with great latency and recall; IVF clusters vectors into lists. Tuning parameters like ef_search or nprobe trades speed for recall. Match the similarity metric to what your embedding model expects, usually cosine.

slides.title: Retrieval Strategies
bullets: Top-k: usually 3-8 chunks
Metadata filtering: restrict by source, date, permissions
Hybrid search: dense vectors + keyword/BM25
Re-ranking: retrieve 20-50, cross-encoder picks best few
MMR: diversity to avoid duplicate chunks
slides.narration: At query time, top-k returns the k most similar chunks — typically three to eight. Metadata filtering narrows the search to relevant sources or respects permissions. Hybrid search combines vector similarity with keyword matching, which is essential for exact terms, names, and codes that embeddings miss. Re-ranking retrieves a wide candidate set then uses a cross-encoder to pick the best few. MMR adds diversity so you don't return near-duplicate passages.

slides.title: Example: Split, Filter, Re-rank
slides.code:
splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(
    chunk_size=600, chunk_overlap=80,
    separators=["\n\n", "\n", ". ", " "])
chunks = splitter.split_documents(docs)

results = vector_store.similarity_search(
    query, k=20, filter={"source": "handbook"})
top = reranker.rerank(query, results)[:5]
slides.narration: Here's the pattern in code. We split documents recursively with a 600-token size and 80-token overlap, falling back through paragraph, line, sentence, and word separators. At query time we retrieve a wide set of twenty candidates filtered to the handbook source, then re-rank and keep the top five. This combination of structure-aware chunking, filtering, and re-ranking dramatically improves relevance over naive top-k.

slides.title: Evaluate and Tune
bullets: Build question / expected-source test pairs
Track Recall@k, context precision, faithfulness
Change ONE variable at a time
Re-embed after changing chunking or model
slides.narration: Don't guess — measure. Create a small evaluation set of questions paired with the source that should answer them. Track recall at k, context precision, and answer faithfulness. When tuning, change one variable at a time so you know what helped. And remember: any change to chunking or the embedding model means you must re-index everything.

slides.title: Common Pitfalls
bullets: Mismatched query/document embedding models
Chunks too large (noise) or too small (lost context)
No metadata → no filtering or citations
Pure vector search for IDs/codes → use hybrid
Forgetting to re-index after parameter changes
slides.narration: Finally, watch for common mistakes: using different embedding models for queries and documents, chunks that are too large or too small, missing metadata that prevents filtering and citations, relying on pure vector search for exact-match queries like IDs where hybrid is needed, and forgetting to re-index after changing parameters. Avoid these and your RAG retrieval will be reliable.
